text:
Beauty in chaos 🎨

This photo from our Chandra X-ray Observatory is the clearest view we have of the remains of an exploded star located in the center of the Milky Way. Scientists can use this view to study how winds from nearby stars have shaped the supernova remnant's evolution.

You could walk on the Moon someday.

We are accepting applications for our next class of astronauts until Dec. 3. Hear about the application process and what it takes from NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell on our episode of “Houston We Have a Podcast.” https://go.nasa.gov/4C7G3xx

text:
Tethys and Dione showed up for the group photo!
 
In addition to the two moons shown here, Saturn has a whole entourage of natural satellites—more than any other planet in our solar system. As of now, the ringed planet has 293 confirmed moons.

text:
How’s that for a starburst?

Found in this distant spiral galaxy is a giant star prone to mysterious outbursts. Thanks to our Chandra X-ray Observatory, scientists identified the culprit behind the eruptions—a hidden companion to the volatile star. https://go.nasa.gov/4eooTSe

page: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
text:
Help us celebrate a historic milestone for Voyager 1.

Next week, our record-setting spacecraft will reach the "one light-day" mark—16 billion miles from Earth, or the time it takes for light to travel in a single day.

We'd like you to share your own light with the universe. On the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17 (your time), grab your phone or flashlight and shine a special Voyager signal into the night sky. Here's how to "Shine Bright" on Voyager's light-day: https://go.nasa.gov/shinebright

We had a great time at MAX POWER — and made a lot of news!

We're recruiting a new class of astronauts, making major advancements on the Moon Base, and challenging students to a $1 million design competition. Catch up with everything we announced at the festival: https://www.nasa.gov/general/max-power-nasas-inaugural-aerospace-expo-ignites-americas-future/

page: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
text:
Just announced at MAX POWER: a $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge! https://go.nasa.gov/3UBpcCs

The competition tasks U.S. high school and post-secondary student teams to develop solutions to real-world engineering constraints for our Artemis missions and establishing a long-term human presence on the Moon.

page: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
text:
Nice shades. 😎

This structure, called a sunshade, will fly on our NEO (Near-Earth Object) Surveyor, a spacecraft that will scout out nearby asteroids and comets that telescopes on the ground might miss.

Above Earth’s atmosphere, NEO Surveyor will be able to spot hard-to-find objects in the direction of the Sun. This sunshade will help by harnessing the Sun’s power and blocking its blinding glare. https://go.nasa.gov/3WsgoPR

page: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
text:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on a six-hour, 59-minute spacewalk today, Nov. 5.

Combined, the eight IROSAs will boost the station's power by up to 30%.

page: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
text:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk (wearing red stripes) are preparing to exit the International Space Station. In today's spacewalk, they'll install the final roll-out solar array, which will boost the station's available power.
